title: Moral persuasion enough for life — parents, princes, magistrates
source_text: XII. Adeoque majori certitudine non opus est ad vitam instituendam. Nec pleraque munia, & officia, quibus vita constat, aliam quam moralem persuasionem in nobis praeexigunt. Nam verbi causa, tantum moraliter certi sumus hos esse nostros parentes cognatos & consanguineos, illos vero esse nostros principes, atque magistratus, quibus tamen in conscientia tenemur ea praestare, quae ejusmodi gradus & dignitas, aut sanguinis conjunctio, jure divino & humano exigit.
pass_a_gloss: And so a greater certainty is not needed for ordering life. Nor do most offices and duties of which life consists presuppose in us any other than moral persuasion. For example’s sake, we are only morally certain that these are our parents, kin, and blood-relations, and that those are our princes and magistrates — to whom yet in conscience we are bound to render what such rank and dignity, or blood-conjunction, exacts by divine and human right.
pass_b_english: Ordering life needs no certainty above moral.
Most life-duties presuppose only moral persuasion.
Parents/kin and princes/magistrates: moral certainty still binds conscience.
